pr_title: Append trailing slash when the path is generated
pr_body:
Fix: https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/43219

Instead of trying to parse the path later to insert the slash or bail out if the path look like it has a format indicator.

**This patch is based on the assumption that `url_for(path: '/blah')` is not an actual public API.** Which isn't something I'm certain of. But at the very least it doesn't seem documented.

### Git History

The `trailing_slash` option was added in https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/db4f421b0bfae226005591b1da90e4b42edf178d. However it was tacked on as a string operation on the return value of the URL Generator.

I don't understand why it wasn't added as an option of the generator itself.

The consequence is that then URL then have to be parsed to know where to insert the slash and wether it is safe or not to do.

https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/8704 fixed a few corner cases and added the following two tests:
```ruby
    assert_equal 'http://www.example.com/books/?q=code', url_for(trailing_slash: true, path: '/books?q=code')
    assert_equal 'http://www.example.com/books/?spareslashes=////', url_for(trailing_slash: true, path: '/books?spareslashes=////')
```

But as far as I can tell they don't correspond to any real behavior. Even if you use `url_for` with the implicit current request arguments as to normalize the current URL, the `path:` option is not passed and the URL generated again from `:controller` and `action`.

issue_context.title: Trailing slashes are not added when url has a dot
issue_context.body:
### Steps to reproduce
create a route that allows dots like in the documentation.

> By default, dynamic segments don't accept dots - this is because the dot is used as a separator for formatted routes. If you need to use a dot within a dynamic segment, add a constraint that overrides this – for example, id: /[^\/]+/ allows anything except a slash.

```ruby
get 'users/:username', to: 'users#show', constraints: { id: /[^\/]+/ }, as: :user, trailing_slash: true
```

call the path with username with and without a dot.

```ruby
user_path('someone')
user_path('some.one')
```
### Expected behavior
both should return  the url with trailing slash
```ruby
user_path('someone')
=> "/users/someone/"
user_path('some.one')
=> "/users/some.one/"
```

### Actual behavior
both should return  the url with trailing slash
```ruby
user_path('someone')
=> "/users/someone/"
user_path('some.one')
=> "/users/some.one"
```

Checking the code, theres a condition that explicitly asks if it has a dot it:

```ruby
def add_trailing_slash(path)
  if path.include?("?")
    path.sub!(/\?/, '/\&')
  elsif !path.include?(".") # here
    path.sub!(/[^\/]\z|\A\z/, '\&/')
  end
end
```

if this is not possible using trailing_slash , how can I achieve it? the problem is that Turbo is not being used if the url has a dot and it does not end in slash (see https://github.com/hotwired/turbo/issues/385)
### System configuration
**Rails version**: 6.1.4

**Ruby version**: 2.7.2-p137
comments:
This behaviour was implemented in https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/14986

In short it's because it assume a `.` is for something like `foo.json`, so it doesn't make sense to append a slash. I can't think of anyway to fix your use case without breaking a larger one.
The “.” check feels naive. Could it not instead check if a format argument is being explicitly passed?

Indeed, it would make much more sense. The problem is there's this other test https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/c839fdb4d715e0866bb4e483283e7e3e60e5bfe1/actionpack/test/dispatch/request_test.rb#L45-L46 which more or less implies that you can pass `url_for(path: "/foo.json?bar=42", trailing_slash: true)`, which is kind of a shitty API if you ask me.

I wouldn't mind getting rid of that, but who knows the kind of code that might depend on this. :/
The PR that introduced this: https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/8704

It sounds like there's a few different scenarios.

If you ask for a URL that contains:

- a "."
- a "?"
- `trailing_slash: true`

Then you should *not* get a trailing slash, because of the querystring. (This is currently supported.)

------------

If you ask for a URL that contains

- a "."
- `trailing_slash: true`
- no "?"
- no specific format

Then you *should* get a trailing slash. (This is the requested change.)

------------

If you ask for a URL that contains

- a "."
- `trailing_slash: true`
- no "?"
- a specific format

Then you should *not* get a trailing slash, because of the format requested. (This is currently supported.)
